planting.note: Direct sow in fall with cold-moist stratification, or plant nursery starts, into fast-draining sandy or rocky soil in full sun; avoid summer irrigation once established.

directions: A mounding coastal native used for erosion control on slopes, rock gardens, and lawn replacement, this buckwheat is a valuable pollinator plant and larval host for several coastal blue butterflies. It tolerates salt spray and wind, making it one of the few shrubby buckwheats suited to immediate coastal bluff plantings — overwatering in heavy clay is the most common failure mode. Let the dried flower heads, which age from white or pink to rust, stand through winter, since they hold seed for finches and continue to look good as a textural element.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall with cold-moist stratification into fast or medium-draining soil in full sun to partial shade; shear back spent flower stalks in late fall.

directions: A classic Northern and Central California coastal bluff native with woolly gray-green foliage and pink-white flower clusters, this buckwheat is an important host plant for several blue butterfly species along the coast. It tolerates clay better than most shrubby Eriogonum and is one of the more shade-tolerant buckwheats, handling partial shade under oaks or in foggy coastal canyons where full-sun species struggle. Shear back spent flower stalks in late fall to keep the woolly mound tidy going into the next bloom cycle.

planting.note: Direct sow with cold stratification, or root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall, into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; avoid rich amended soil, which causes legginess.

directions: A Channel Islands endemic with showy dark rose-red to magenta flower pompons held on branching stalks well above gray-green spoon-shaped foliage, this is one of the most ornamentally striking native buckwheats and a strong butterfly and bee draw. As an island-endemic species it is somewhat less cold-tolerant and more forgiving of light afternoon shade than mainland desert buckwheats, so it is best suited to coastal and near-coastal gardens rather than hard-freeze inland sites. It flowers nearly continuously from late spring through fall, making it a strong choice for border edges, rock gardens, and containers.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Direct sow with cold stratification, or root semi-hardwood cuttings, giving the shrub 4-5 feet of lateral space; good drainage and minimal summer water are essential.

directions: A fast-growing silvery-gray coastal shrub, this species is an exceptional butterfly-garden plant documented as a nectar source for Acmon Blue, Mormon Metalmark, Umber Skipper, Gray Hairstreak, and Great Purple Hairstreak, and a larval host for the Square-spotted Blue. Because it blooms in winter, spring, summer, and fall almost simultaneously, it functions as a near-continuous nectar source in a habitat garden. It is naturally a beach-and-bluff plant, so good drainage and minimal summer water are essential — wet feet in clay soil is the main killer in cultivation.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Direct sow with cold stratification into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, planted behind lower mounding buckwheats so its tall late display reads above them.

directions: A gray-leaved mounding buckwheat topped by tall leafless wand-like flower stems that bloom from August through November, this species is a rare late-season nectar source for pollinators and migrating butterflies when most other natives have finished. Plant it specifically to extend bloom succession in a native or pollinator garden, since its value is almost entirely in timing — nothing else in the genus blooms this late. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and resents any supplemental summer water, which can shorten its lifespan.

planting.note: Direct sow with 4-6 weeks cold stratification mimicking desert winter chilling into sharply drained rocky or gravel soil in full sun.

directions: An intricately branched desert subshrub with fine wiry stems and small white-to-pink flowers, this species is valuable for xeriscape and desert-native gardens where most showier coastal buckwheats fail, and useful for erosion control on rocky slopes. Native to Mojave and Great Basin foothill woodland, pinyon-juniper, and Joshua tree communities, it needs sharp drainage and tolerates both summer heat and winter cold far better than coastal Eriogonum species. Its finely branched, almost leafless silhouette makes it a good structural accent among rock and gravel rather than a foliage plant.

planting.note: Direct sow with 6-8 weeks cold stratification into lean gritty mineral soil with sharp drainage and no rich organic amendment; patience is required, as mats take several seasons to bulk up.

directions: A tight, woody, mat-forming cushion plant with small gray fuzzy leaves and round flower heads that age from pale yellow to pink and orange, this species is widely recommended as an outstanding rock garden and trough subject by alpine garden specialists. It is a genuine high-elevation Great Basin cushion plant, demanding the classic rock-garden formula of lean gritty mineral soil and full sun, and is markedly more cold-hardy than the coastal California buckwheats. Once established the dense mats are extremely long-lived and need essentially no summer water.

planting.note: Direct sow with 6-8 weeks cold stratification into dry rocky or sandy soil in full sun, built for cold winters rather than mild coastal conditions.

directions: Native from sagebrush and juniper flats up into ponderosa pine forest, this compact subshrub carries globe-shaped flower heads and is well suited to rock gardens and sagebrush-steppe-style plantings in interior climates too cold or dry for California coastal buckwheats. It forms a woody caudex that sends up erect flowering stems in early summer, giving a tidier, more upright profile than the prostrate mat-forming buckwheats. It is a solid choice for a Great Basin or high-desert themed rock garden alongside sagebrush and native penstemons.
sources: Burke Herbarium Image Collection (University of Washington)
